speechtext: We have been urging that.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I hope the minister will continue because I think that is a very essential thing to do. When the minister is urging that, he might also perhaps realize that there are certain other changes in the United Nations that should take place. If it is going to become an effective body, a more liberal interpretation must be made of the charter. There must be expansion of existing machinery and the adding of new bodies in addition to those 1 have already mentioned.
We must give to the administrative body of the United Nations authority in areas not now under national sovereignty. I mention outer space as one of these. There must be greater use made of the international court of justice and the development of international law, perhaps by the creation of certain existing tribunals as ad hoc tribunals from which appeals might be pressed to the international court of justice.
We must, of course, adhere to the principle of universality of membership notwithstanding what the difficulties are, as we well knew in 1955. We must make the United Nations less dependent for its income than it is now. We must not have the shameful situation that confronted it last week, when seemingly it had to beg for money to carry on in the Congo operations that were in the interests of all people of the world as well as the people of that troubled country.
Then we must press, as Mr. Nehru said, for charter revision at the appropriate time, and he thought that the time certainly had not come when he spoke last fall. So that I think while we support the United Nations we must recognize the dangers that confront it.
I see that Mr. Hamilton Fish Armstrong has suggested recently in penetrating observations that this crisis of the United Nations is one to which some nations in the west have not fully addressed themselves. He is concerned about this particular situation. He envisages the possibility of the Soviet union establishing her own international forum, if she cannot get her own way at the United Nations, as presently constituted. Whether or not that eventuates, no one can tell but these are dangerous situations, not only in the various places we have mentioned, Laos, the Caribbean, Germany and so on, but right in the United Nations itself we have a crisis. We are not going to resolve that crisis by being evangelistic about what the United Nations has done, but by recognizing the challenge that is presented to us right in the
External Affairs
United Nations and making it an effective body. If there is no United Nations in the kind of world in which we live, with the kind of instruments of war which now persist I, for one, and I am sure this represents the opinion of every member of this house, cannot believe the peace of the world in this interdependent period can possibly be maintained only by a balance of power system.
Disarmament has been a worthy objective of the minister. Certainly he has found since his period of service as Secretary of State for External Affairs that the optimism which characterized his earlier speeches in this field has not been justified. He perhaps now recognizes that the facts of life are not as simple or as noble as they appeared, when he undertook the very heavy responsibility which he now discharges so honourably and so sincerely. The fact is that good wishes and sincerity are no substitute for wise policies in the kind of ruthless world in which we live today.
The Soviet union has affirmed its willingness, as of a few weeks ago, to reach an agreement in the matter of the cessation of nuclear tests. Last year the minister told us that there were great prospects for agreement in this area and that if we got agreement, we would have an opportunity for progress in the broader field of disarmament. My suggestion is that the events of today indicate that whatever justification there may have been for hope in that field is rapidly being dissipated. I hope this is not the case, but I know of no other interpretation to put on the words which Mr. Khrushchev addressed to Mr. Walter Lipp-mann as reported last week. It may be that the Soviet union is now determined to make the nuclear talks part of a package deal in connection with the whole question of disarmament. In any event, the fact is- this is no fault of Canada or, I believe, basically of most of the nations in the west-we have made no progress in this field. No progress was made when we were in office, and no progress is being made now. Procedural achievements and procedural initiatives are not real progress.
I believe that we must pursue this objective of disarmament. Even many of the experts, on whose judgment and experience we rely, now have abandoned the word "disarmament". They are now talking about arms control. I suggest to the minister that the job of the statesman is to keep the higher objective of disarmament, even though there may be a realization of how difficult that is going to be, particularly in the face of the fact that there is no known scientific method for the determination of the existence of undisclosed nuclear weapons. The minister says

External Affairs
that the policy of this government is to continue to advocate the cessation of nuclear tests with or without controls; that is the position he has reaffirmed today, although he did point out that the resolution put forward by Ireland, which Canada supported, provides as far as this country is concerned for a limited period in which Canada will withhold a decision as to the use of nuclear weapons in Canada.
There is a conflict, undoubtedly. I do not expect the minister to admit it between the pronouncements made by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Harkness) and those made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs with regard to this matter. The minister is clear when he states that the policy of the government is that there should be no nuclear tests, underground or overground, with or without controls. However, that is not what one has a right to interpret as being the view of the Minister of National Defence. I can only hope that in this matter the minister will be able to establish his position vis-a-vis his colleagues and, in particular, in his discussions with the Minister of National Defence.
A few moments ago an hon. member asked me what further Canada could do. I have indicated, I believe, that we could have gone further. I believe we could go further now and put forward a specific plan which may or may not be accepted but which, in our name and supported by certain nations, might have a persuasive influence, even though it might not bring about full results. It is worth the try.
If general disarmament is to be attained, it is certainly not going to be achieved easily. We might as well recognize this now. All one has to do is to read what men like Kissinger and Kohn have to say, to realize what has developed in connection with modern nuclear weapons, to appreciate what a tremendous job mankind is going to have in the attempt to unscramble the nuclear paraphernalia that has been devised. We should give consideration to other plans that have to be devised if we are going to have disarmament.
We should give consideration, for example, to the kind of thing I mentioned in passing a few minutes ago. What type of international police force should be established to preserve international peace and security? What principles of international law should govern such forces? What internal security forces, in precise terms, would be required by the nations of the world if existing armaments were abolished? These are questions that we have to consider. The United Nations emergency force was understandably established without any opportunity for prepara-

tion on the part of the secretariat. However, as we know now from the Congo operations, the United Nations secretariat, as presently constituted, is not in a position to provide the kind of administrative services that make such a United Nations force fully effective.
This is the kind of constructive suggestion to which we might well give careful consideration and thereby make a definite contribution of our own. There are so many other areas one could traverse, but my time is nearly exhausted. I simply want to go back to where I began by saying that these problems, the United Nations, disarmament, the organization of American states, together with the turbulent situations that now exist in so many areas, point up the difficulties that attend mankind at this time. It is not easy, we all know, to see our way clear through this situation. A nation-or group of nations-that is reluctant to use force, that is reluctant to follow the concept of even evolutionary international law, encounters difficulty when it is confronted with irresponsible actions by nations bent on implanting in the minds of men their philosophy of life. This is a very difficult situation. This is what concerns us. Statesmanship of the highest order is required in all of the countries, and our country no less than others has a responsibility. We must pursue the ideals of a world under international law but we must do so realistically, realizing what are the pitfalls; we must do so realizing that obviously, in face of the November conference in Moscow, no agreement is going to be made that does not meet at this stage of international relations the particular policy objective of the Soviet union.
I admit, of course, that we cannot leap over a chasm with one bound. This procedure has been tried previously and the results have been fatal. However, I believe that the prime minister of the United Kingdom was right when he said in Boston that the nations of the west, without violating their right to individual opinion, must recognize that at this time it is essential that there be a strong measure of prudent unity among the western powers. If we have this unity; if we have a firm will to attack vigorously our agenda of economic development, not only in terms of our relations with the common market through
O.E.C.D. and the like but the economic development of other people in the world who are going to have a decision as to which of the great ideologies shall prevail; if we can strengthen the United Nations along the lines that are envisaged not as stated by me necessarily but as outlined by others who share

these views rather than yielding to the destructive purposes of those who want to use the United Nations only for their purposes and for the furtherance of their aims, we may find that the road may be easier. If we can apply as much time and money in studying for peace as we do in planning for war; if, to use C. P. Snow's phrase, we can regain our "appetite" for the future-and I would say our soul as well-then we shall be true to the values of our own way of life and contribute to a more peaceful world.
The minister has an extremely difficult assignment. We respect that difficulty. However, we urge him now to appreciate, as I am sure he does-although I feel that he did not give us evidence of this today-the urgency that attends us and to indicate in bold and clear terms something that represents the character and the wishes of our people along the lines spoken of by people like C. P. Snow, Barbara Ward and other strong protagonists of the western position. That is the kind of leadership we need at this time, not only here at home but throughout the west and throughout the world.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure we all listened with great interest to the minister's review of international affairs and the work of this department. We all recognize the problems he faces at the present time possibly to a greater degree than ever before. We have great respect for the minister and we appreciate the work being done by his officials around the world. Although called away for a few minutes, I also listened with interest to the very eloquent remarks of the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) but I do not agree with all he said.
External Affairs
I have listened to a great many reviews of international affairs from our secretaries of state for external affairs. I noticed that today for the first time the minister referred to himself as a foreign minister. I understand that, according to British tradition, a foreign minister always wears a top hat on formal occasions. Possibly we shall see him doing that in the future. However, while I was listening to the minister I was thinking about the two wars. There are in this house members who marched to war in the first world war and in the second one. In the first world war our battle was to save the world for democracy and in the second world war it was to fight against nazi tyranny and to bring about a system of world peace. Between the first and second world wars the statemen of the world lost numerous opportunities to bring about and develop that peace in the world.
One reading the history of the world between the first and second world wars realizes how, just through the lack of imagination or the lack of wisdom on the part of a very few people, the tide was turned in the wrong direction. Since the second world war, at the conclusion of which we all had high hopes, some nations have made various mistakes. The minister said that we should give the government our backing. We give the government our backing. He said the government recognizes its opportunity but also its responsibility. We give this government our backing if it recognizes its opportunity and its responsibility in relation to that large group of nations outside this major struggle between the two great nations of the east and the west. Mr. Speaker, may I call it six o'clock.

SMALL BUSINESS LOAN APPLICATIONS- FORT WILLIAM
speechtext:
1.	Has any application for loans to small businesses been received by chartered banks in the constituency of Fort William since the passing of legislation under Bill C-40?
2.	How many loans have been made, if any, and the amount of each?
3.	Were any applications turned down, and, if so, what were the reasons?
Answer by:	Hon. Donald M. Fleming
(Minister of Finance):
1, 2 and 3. Information not available.
